title: 8-Week-Old Puppy Schedule: Daily Routine + Free Printable PDF
description: A realistic 8-week-old puppy schedule: a sample hour-by-hour day, meals, potty breaks, naps and bedtime, with sources and a free printable PDF.
excerpt: A sample day for an 8-week-old puppy, built from AKC, PDSA and RSPCA guidance, with a free printable schedule and daily log.

html:
An 8-week-old puppy needs about four meals, a potty trip every hour or two while awake, a nap roughly every hour and a very short training game or two, all in a repeating loop. That is the pattern the sources below agree on. This guide turns it into a sample day you can copy, plus a free printable PDF with a daily log.

How to read this guide

Facts with a source name come from the pages listed at the end (AKC, PDSA, RSPCA, Dogs Trust). Anything marked (general guidance) is common trainer advice that we could not confirm in those sources. Your puppy, your home and your vet come first. Puppies of the same age can differ a lot.

The 8-week-old puppy day at a glance

WhatWhat to plan for
MealsFour a day. AKC says most puppies eat four meals daily between 6 and 12 weeks. Follow your food’s feeding guide and your vet.
Potty tripsAKC says very young puppies often need to go out every one to two hours while awake. RSPCA suggests every 45 minutes to an hour at first, and PDSA suggests every 2 to 3 hours in the day. Start at the short end and stretch slowly.
SleepAKC says puppies usually sleep 18 to 20 hours a day. A puppy may nap about every hour, for 30 minutes up to two hours.
Play and trainingVery short and happy: about 1 to 5 minutes at a time (general guidance).
Crate or pen timePDSA says never longer than three hours at a time for a crate. At 8 weeks, start with a few minutes and build up.
NightPlan for one or two quiet potty trips. AKC says puppies are often not ready to sleep through the night.

Why so many potty trips? AKC points out that most puppies come home around 8 weeks old, which is when bladder control is at its weakest. That is normal, not a training failure.

Sample day: hour by hour

This is an example only, not a prescribed routine. Move the times to fit your family and keep the order: wake, potty, activity, potty, rest. The meal times below are about four hours apart (general guidance).

Time (example)What happensWhy
6:30Wake up. Straight outside to potty. Reward right away.Puppies usually need to go after sleep (AKC lists waking up as a potty moment).
7:00Breakfast, then another potty trip soon after.AKC lists eating as a potty moment.
7:30Play and a 1 to 2 minute training game (name game, treat for coming to you).Short, happy sessions (general guidance).
8:00Potty, then a nap in the crate or pen.AKC says puppies usually nap after play.
9:30Wake up. Potty first, then gentle exploring in a safe, puppy-proofed space.Potty after waking, every time.
10:15Chew toy, sniffing, a short cuddle.Calm activity, not wild play.
10:45Potty, then nap.Do not wait for a tired puppy to melt down.
11:30Wake, potty, lunch, potty.Meal two of four.
12:15Calm play, a short handling game (touch paws and ears for a second, then a treat).Gentle handling helps later at the vet (general guidance).
12:45Potty, then nap.Rest follows activity.
2:30Wake, potty, play with a safe toy.Check the clock: more than two hours since the last trip?
3:30Afternoon meal, potty.Meal three of four.
4:00Short training game, then a tiny outing in your own yard or on a blanket (ask your vet when it is safe to go to public places).Vaccine timing differs, so ask your vet.
4:30Potty, then nap.
6:00Wake, potty, calm play and a chew.Evening wild patches are common (see puppy zoomies).
7:30Dinner, then potty.Meal four of four, a few hours before bed.
8:00Quiet family time, gentle chewing, lights lower.Wind down.
9:30Last potty trip, then to bed in the crate or pen close to you.Right before bed is a potty moment (AKC).
NightIf your puppy wakes and needs to go: calmly carry them out, praise quietly, put them straight back to sleep.AKC describes this exact approach for night potty breaks.

Working during the day? Our guide for working owners shows how to cover the middle of the day, and can you leave a puppy alone for 8 hours? covers the hard limits.

The loop behind the clock

You do not need to watch the clock all day. Run this loop (general guidance):

  1. Wake and go straight outside.
  2. Meal or activity (play, a training game, sniffing).
  3. Potty again after eating or playing.
  4. Nap in a quiet, safe spot.
  5. Repeat.

If your puppy naps for 45 minutes, your day moves earlier. If a nap runs two hours, it moves later. The order stays the same.

Meals at 8 weeks

AKC says four feedings a day is a common guideline and that puppies are usually on four meals between 6 and 12 weeks, then three meals from about 3 months. Feed at regular times in regular amounts. For the amount, read the feeding guide on your puppy food and ask your vet. We cover this in detail in puppy feeding schedule.

Potty breaks: how often really?

The sources give different numbers, and all of them can be right for different puppies:

  • AKC: every one to two hours while awake, plus after waking, eating, drinking, playing and before bed.
  • RSPCA: about every 45 minutes to an hour at first, depending on age.
  • PDSA: every 2 to 3 hours in the day.

A simple way to choose (general guidance): take your puppy out at the five key moments and whenever an hour has passed. Watch for sniffing, circling and whining. If accidents are frequent, go back to the shorter gap. Our potty training schedule and puppy won’t pee outside guides go deeper.

Naps and bedtime

  • Plan active time, then quiet time. AKC suggests following play with rest.
  • Safe sleeping spot. A crate, a bed or a quiet corner. AKC says to leave a sleeping puppy alone.
  • Watch for overtired. AKC warns that too much stimulation and exhaustion can lead to unwanted behavior. A biting, zooming puppy at 6 pm is often a tired puppy.
  • Dim and quiet at bedtime. AKC suggests low light and low volume as a sleep cue.

More detail: puppy nap and sleep schedule.

Play and training: tiny sessions

At 8 weeks, think seconds and minutes, not half-hours. Pick one tiny goal per session (general guidance): say your puppy’s name and give a treat when they look at you, reward a sit, or practice coming to you. End while your puppy is still keen. See first commands to teach a puppy. Meeting new sounds and people calmly counts as training too: puppy socialization checklist.

Alone time and the crate

PDSA says a crate should never be used for longer than three hours at a time, and Dogs Trust says to introduce crates slowly and in the puppy’s own time. At 8 weeks, begin with short practice while you are in the house: a few minutes with a chew, then a little longer. New to crates? Read crate training a puppy.

The first nights

Expect crying and a potty trip in the night. Keep it calm and boring: potty, quiet praise, back to sleep. We explain what to check in puppy crying at night and set up the first night in puppy’s first night home.

When the schedule falls apart

Travel, visitors, a vet visit and a bad night all happen. Go back to the loop at the next wake-up. Do not try to make up missed sleep or meals. If your puppy seems unusually sleepy, will not eat, or has repeated diarrhea or vomiting, call your vet. This guide is general information, not veterinary advice.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting for the puppy to ask. At 8 weeks they often do not signal until it is too late.
  • Long play sessions with no nap. Overtired puppies bite and zoom.
  • Skipping the potty trip after waking up or eating.
  • Making the crate a punishment.
  • Comparing your puppy to someone else’s. Ranges are wide.

Free printable: 8-week-old puppy daily schedule and log

We made a 2-page PDF: page one is the sample day as a tick-box checklist, page two is a blank daily log for potty trips, meals, naps and notes. Print it, put it on the fridge and fill it in for a week. You will see your own puppy’s pattern, which is more useful than any template. Use the form below to get it by email.
quick: At 8 weeks plan about four meals, a potty trip every hour or two while awake, a nap about every hour (18 to 20 hours of sleep in total), 1 to 5 minute training games and one or two quiet potty trips at night. Use the sample day as a pattern, not a strict clock.

faq.q: How many meals should an 8-week-old puppy eat a day?
faq.a: AKC says most puppies eat four meals a day between 6 and 12 weeks. Follow your puppy food’s feeding guide and ask your vet about amounts.

faq.q: How often should an 8-week-old puppy go out to pee?
faq.a: AKC says very young puppies often need to go out every one to two hours while awake, plus after waking, eating, drinking, playing and before bed. RSPCA suggests 45 minutes to an hour at first, and PDSA suggests every 2 to 3 hours in the day. Start with the shorter gap and stretch it as your puppy grows.

faq.q: How long does an 8-week-old puppy sleep?
faq.a: AKC says puppies usually sleep 18 to 20 hours a day, with naps about every hour that last from 30 minutes to two hours.

faq.q: Will my 8-week-old puppy sleep through the night?
faq.a: AKC says puppies are sometimes not yet ready to sleep through the night and may need a potty break. We did not find a fixed age in the sources, so plan for one or two quiet trips and ask your vet if you are unsure.

faq.q: Can an 8-week-old puppy be left alone?
faq.a: Only for very short, practiced periods. PDSA says a crate should never be used for longer than three hours at a time, and young puppies need frequent potty trips. See our guide on leaving a puppy alone.

faq.q: Do I have to follow the schedule exactly?
faq.a: No. Keep the order (wake, potty, activity, potty, rest) and adjust the clock. Puppies differ, and the times in our sample day are examples.
